pages.title: LINEAR & LOGISTIC REGRESSION
pages.subtitle: Fit a line, then bend it into a probability
pages.learner: How can a line predict yes or no?

panels.heading: Linear Regression: Fit a Line
panels.body:
Predict a number: y_hat = w0 + w1*x1 + ... + wd*xd.
Residual = y - y_hat.
Least squares picks weights that minimize MSE (mean squared error) = average residual^2.
panels.diagram: Scatter plot of house size (m^2) vs price with a cyan fitted line; vertical amber residual segments from each point to the line, a few drawn as small squares to show 'squared error'.

panels.heading: Closed Form vs Gradient Descent
panels.body:
Normal equation: w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y. Exact, one shot.
Gradient descent: w <- w - lr * gradient. Iterative; scales to huge or streaming data.
Libraries use QR/SVD, not a raw inverse.
panels.diagram: Split panel: left a single arrow 'X, y -> formula -> w' labeled EXACT; right a bowl-shaped loss surface with a zig-zag path of dots descending to the minimum labeled ITERATIVE.

panels.heading: Assumptions to Check
panels.body:
Linear relationship (after any feature transforms).
Independent errors, constant variance: no funnel in residuals.
No strong multicollinearity: correlated features make weights unstable.
Normal errors matter only for p-values and intervals.
panels.diagram: Two small residual-vs-prediction plots: GOOD = random flat cloud around zero (lime check); BAD = funnel widening to the right and a curved band (orange X).

panels.heading: Logistic Regression: Bend to 0-1
panels.body:
For classes: p = sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), z = w.x + b.
z is the log-odds: log(p / (1 - p)).
Train with log loss; no closed form.
Boundary: z = 0 (p = 0.5), a straight line or plane.
panels.diagram: Top: S-shaped sigmoid curve, x-axis z from -6 to 6, y-axis p from 0 to 1, dashed line at p = 0.5 meeting z = 0. Bottom: 2D scatter of two colored classes split by a straight cyan boundary line labeled 'z = 0'.

panels.heading: Reading the Coefficients
panels.body:
Linear: +1 unit of x -> y changes by w (others held fixed).
Logistic: +1 unit of x -> log-odds +w, odds multiply by e^w.
Compare sizes only after standardizing.
Coefficients show association, not cause.
panels.diagram: Two labeled dials: 'linear w = 3 -> +3 per unit' and 'logistic w = 0.7 -> odds x2.0'; a small warning tag 'not causal'.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Pass the Exam
panels.body:
Model: z = -4 + 1.5 * hours.
2 hours: z = -1 -> p = 0.27.
4 hours: z = 2 -> p = 0.88.
Boundary: z = 0 at 2.67 hours. Each extra hour multiplies the odds by e^1.5 = 4.5.
panels.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
clf.predict_proba(X_new)[:, 1]
panels.diagram: Sigmoid plotted against study hours 0-6 with marked points (2 h, 0.27) and (4 h, 0.88); vertical dashed boundary at 2.67 h; small table of hours / z / p.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Extrapolating outside the training range.
Outliers drag least squares: check residuals or use Huber loss.
Separable classes: weights blow up; regularize.
0.5 threshold is a default: tune it to error costs.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons beside four mini sketches: a line shooting past the data, one outlier tilting the fit, an infinitely steep sigmoid, a threshold slider.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
A logistic weight is 0.7. What happens to the odds per unit of x?
Answer: x e^0.7, about double.
panels.diagram: Robot holding a quiz card with the question; the answer printed upside down in a small corner box.

pages.footer: Linear predicts a number; logistic predicts log-odds, then squashes them into a probability.
pages.summary: Explains linear regression (least squares, normal equation vs gradient descent, assumptions) and logistic regression (sigmoid, log-odds, decision boundary), how to read their coefficients, with a worked pass/fail example and common pitfalls.

pages.title: TREES & ENSEMBLES CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: From one decision tree to a winning forest
pages.learner: Why do trees beat my neural net?

panels.heading: How a Decision Tree Splits
panels.body:
Ask yes/no questions: income > 50k? age < 30?
Each split picks the feature + threshold that makes children purest.
Leaves predict the majority class (or the mean for regression).
No scaling needed.
panels.diagram: Small tree diagram: root 'income > 50k?' branching yes/no to 'age < 30?' and leaf nodes colored by class (lime = approve, orange = deny).

panels.heading: Gini vs Entropy
panels.body:
Gini = 1 - sum(p_k^2). Entropy = -sum(p_k * log2 p_k).
50/50 node: Gini 0.5, entropy 1.0. Pure node: both 0.
Gain = parent impurity - weighted child impurity.
Nearly identical splits; Gini is a bit faster.
panels.diagram: Plot of impurity vs fraction of class 1 (0 to 1): entropy curve peaking at 1.0 and Gini curve peaking at 0.5, both zero at the ends.

panels.heading: Worked Example: One Split
panels.body:
Parent: 10 emails, 5 spam -> Gini 0.5.
Split on 'has link': left 4 spam / 1 ham, right 1 spam / 4 ham.
Each child: 1 - (0.8^2 + 0.2^2) = 0.32.
Gain = 0.5 - 0.32 = 0.18.
panels.diagram: Parent box with 5 red + 5 blue envelope icons splitting into two child boxes (4 red/1 blue and 1 red/4 blue), each annotated with its Gini value.

panels.heading: Depth Controls Overfitting
panels.body:
Deep tree: memorizes noise (high variance).
Shallow tree: too simple (high bias).
Limit max_depth or min_samples_leaf, or prune with ccp_alpha.
panels.diagram: Two decision-region maps of the same 2D points: depth 2 = few big rectangles; depth 20 = jagged tiny boxes around single points.

panels.heading: Bagging & Random Forests
panels.body:
Bagging = bootstrap aggregating: train trees on resampled rows, average their votes.
Random forest also samples features at each split -> less correlated trees.
Cuts variance; out-of-bag rows give a free validation score.
panels.diagram: Dataset fanning out into 4 bootstrap samples, each feeding a different small tree, arrows converging into a 'vote / average' box.

panels.heading: Boosting: Fix the Errors
panels.body:
Build shallow trees in sequence; each fits the residual errors (gradients) of the ensemble so far.
A small learning rate plus early stopping prevents overfitting.
Tools: XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost.
panels.code:
from lightgbm import LGBMClassifier
m = LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=500, learning_rate=0.05)
m.fit(X_train, y_train)
panels.diagram: Chain of three small trees left to right, each followed by a shrinking 'residual' bar chart; plus signs between trees summing into a final prediction.

panels.heading: Feature Importance Pitfalls
panels.body:
Impurity importance favors high-cardinality features (IDs!) and uses training data.
Correlated features split the credit.
Prefer permutation importance on held-out data, or SHAP values.
Important does not mean causal.
panels.diagram: Bar chart where 'customer_id' has the tallest bar stamped with an orange 'FAKE' warning; beside it a held-out permutation chart where it drops to near zero.

panels.heading: When Trees Beat Neural Nets
panels.body:
Tabular data: mixed types, skewed features, missing values.
Boosted trees often win with less tuning and compute.
Neural nets win on images, text, audio.
panels.diagram: Scoreboard: 'spreadsheet data -> boosted trees', 'images / text / audio -> neural nets'.

pages.footer: One tree overfits; bagging averages away variance; boosting chips away bias.
pages.summary: Shows how decision trees choose splits (Gini, entropy, information gain) with a worked example, how depth controls overfitting, how random forests (bagging) and gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) combine trees, why feature importances mislead, and why trees still win on tabular data.

pages.title: SVM, KNN & NAIVE BAYES
pages.subtitle: Three classic classifiers and when each shines
pages.learner: Which one should I try first?

panels.heading: SVM: The Widest Margin
panels.body:
SVM = support vector machine.
Find the boundary w.x + b = 0 with the widest gap to both classes: margin = 2 / ||w||.
Only the closest points, the support vectors, define it.
panels.diagram: Two classes of dots separated by a cyan line with dashed parallel margin lines on each side; the few points touching the dashed lines are circled and labeled 'support vectors'; double arrow labeled 'margin'.

panels.heading: Soft Margin & C
panels.body:
Real classes overlap, so allow violations (hinge loss).
Large C: punish errors hard -> narrow margin, may overfit.
Small C: tolerate errors -> wider margin, smoother boundary.
panels.diagram: Side-by-side: 'C = 100' tight margin bending to every point; 'C = 0.1' wide margin with a few points inside it.

panels.heading: The Kernel Trick
panels.body:
Map points to a space where they separate linearly, without computing the map: only k(x, x') is needed.
RBF kernel: k = exp(-gamma * ||x - x'||^2).
Rings in 2D separate once you add z = x1^2 + x2^2.
panels.code:
from sklearn.svm import SVC
SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1.0, gamma="scale")
panels.diagram: Left: two concentric rings of points in 2D. Arrow 'lift with z = x1^2 + x2^2' to the right: the same points on a 3D bowl, cut by a flat plane.

panels.heading: k-Nearest Neighbors
panels.body:
k-NN: no training, just store the data.
Predict by majority vote (or mean) of the k closest points.
Small k: noisy. Large k: blurry. Odd k avoids ties for 2 classes.
Distance: Euclidean, Manhattan, or cosine for text.
panels.diagram: A query star surrounded by colored dots; circle around its 3 nearest neighbors (2 blue, 1 red -> blue) and a larger circle for k = 7 with a different vote.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Why Scale
panels.body:
Features: income (0-200,000) and age (0-100).
Unscaled, a 1,000 income gap outweighs a 40-year age gap.
Standardize: z = (x - mean) / std, so each feature counts fairly.
panels.diagram: Two scatter plots of the same points: unscaled = squashed into a thin horizontal strip; scaled = round cloud; the nearest neighbor of the query changes between them.

panels.heading: Naive Bayes
panels.body:
Bayes rule: P(class | x) is proportional to P(class) * product of P(x_i | class).
Naive: features assumed independent given the class.
Wrong, yet strong for text: fast, little data needed.
Laplace smoothing (+1) stops unseen words zeroing everything.
panels.diagram: Formula banner with the prior and likelihood terms colored differently; small bag-of-words icons multiplying together.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Spam Filter
panels.body:
Prior: P(spam) = 0.4, P(ham) = 0.6.
Word 'free': P(free | spam) = 0.3, P(free | ham) = 0.02.
Scores: spam 0.4 x 0.3 = 0.12; ham 0.6 x 0.02 = 0.012.
P(spam | free) = 0.12 / 0.132 = 0.91.
panels.diagram: Email with the word 'free' highlighted; two score bars (spam 0.12 tall, ham 0.012 tiny) feeding a gauge reading 91% spam.

panels.heading: Compare & Pitfalls
panels.body:
SVM: strong in high dimensions; kernels slow past ~100k rows.
k-NN: no training, slow predictions.
Naive Bayes: fastest text baseline; overconfident.
Pitfall: unscaled features break SVM and k-NN.
panels.diagram: Three-row comparison table with columns training speed / prediction speed / needs scaling / best for, using lime and orange icons.

pages.footer: SVM draws the widest road, k-NN asks the neighbors, Naive Bayes counts the evidence.
pages.summary: Compares three classic classifiers: support vector machines (margin, support vectors, C, kernel trick), k-nearest neighbors (choice of k, distance, why scaling matters) and Naive Bayes (independence assumption, spam example), with a when-to-use table and pitfalls.

pages.title: CLUSTERING CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Finding groups when nobody gave you labels
pages.learner: How many clusters are really there?

panels.heading: k-Means Step by Step
panels.body:
Unsupervised: group points with no labels.
1. Pick k centroids. 2. Assign each point to its nearest centroid.
3. Move each centroid to its points' mean. 4. Repeat until stable.
Minimizes inertia = sum of squared distances to centroids.
panels.diagram: Four mini frames in a row: random centroids (X marks), points colored by nearest X, X marks sliding to cluster centers, final stable clusters.

panels.heading: Worked Example: 1D, k = 2
panels.body:
Points: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 12. Start centroids: 1 and 2.
Assign: {1} and {2, 3, 10, 11, 12} -> means 1 and 7.6.
Reassign: {1, 2, 3} and {10, 11, 12} -> means 2 and 11.
No change: converged.
panels.diagram: Number line 0-13 with six dots; two rows showing centroid markers moving from (1, 2) to (1, 7.6) to (2, 11), with dots recolored each round.

panels.heading: k-Means++ & Choosing k
panels.body:
k-means++: pick each new start centroid far from existing ones -> better, faster. Run several restarts.
Elbow: plot inertia vs k, pick the bend.
Silhouette = (b - a) / max(a, b), from -1 to 1: higher = better separated.
panels.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
KMeans(n_clusters=3, init="k-means++", n_init=10)
panels.diagram: Left: elbow curve of inertia vs k = 1..8 with the bend at k = 3 circled. Right: silhouette score vs k with its peak at k = 3.

panels.heading: Hierarchical Clustering
panels.body:
Agglomerative: start with every point alone; merge the two closest clusters, repeat.
Linkage: single (min), complete (max), average, Ward (least variance increase).
Cut the dendrogram at a height to get any number of clusters.
panels.diagram: Dendrogram over 8 labeled points with a dashed horizontal cut line producing 3 colored clusters.

panels.heading: DBSCAN: Density Wins
panels.body:
DBSCAN = density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise.
Core point: at least min_samples points within radius eps.
Clusters grow through connected core points; the rest is noise.
Any shape, no k needed.
panels.diagram: Two crescent 'moons' of points correctly colored as two clusters, a few gray isolated points marked 'noise', one point with a dashed eps circle around it.

panels.heading: Gaussian Mixture Models
panels.body:
GMM: each cluster is a Gaussian with its own mean and covariance.
Fit with EM (expectation-maximization).
Soft assignment: a point can be 70% A, 30% B.
Handles elliptical clusters; choose k with BIC.
panels.diagram: Two overlapping tilted ellipses (contour lines) over points; one point between them labeled '70% A / 30% B'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Unscaled features: the largest unit dominates distance.
k-means assumes round, similar-size clusters; fails on moons and rings.
k-means returns k clusters even for pure noise.
DBSCAN struggles when densities vary.
panels.diagram: Orange warning frame: k-means wrongly slicing two moons in half with a straight line, versus DBSCAN getting them right.

pages.footer: Scale first, match the algorithm to the cluster shape, then sanity-check the groups.
pages.summary: Covers unsupervised clustering: the k-means algorithm with a worked 1D trace, k-means++ initialization, choosing k with the elbow and silhouette methods, hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, Gaussian mixture models, and common pitfalls like scaling and non-spherical clusters.

pages.title: DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Fewer dimensions, same story
pages.learner: Why does my t-SNE plot mislead me?

panels.heading: Curse of Dimensionality
panels.body:
Each new feature multiplies the volume of space: data gets sparse.
10 bins per feature: 2D = 100 cells, 10D = 10 billion.
Distances concentrate: nearest and farthest points look alike.
k-NN and clustering suffer first.
panels.diagram: Grid sequence: 1D line with 10 cells, 2D square with 100 cells, 3D cube with 1,000 cells, the same 20 dots looking ever sparser.

panels.heading: PCA: Find the Main Axes
panels.body:
PCA = principal component analysis.
Center the data, compute the covariance matrix.
Eigenvectors = new orthogonal axes (principal components); eigenvalues = variance along each.
Keep the top k and project onto them.
panels.diagram: Tilted elliptical cloud of 2D points with two perpendicular arrows from the center: long arrow 'PC1' along the spread, short arrow 'PC2'; points projected as ticks onto PC1.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Explained Variance
panels.body:
Eigenvalues: 4.0, 2.5, 1.0, 0.5 (total 8).
Shares: 50%, 31%, 13%, 6%.
PC1 + PC2 keep 81% of the variance with half the dimensions.
Rule of thumb: keep 90-95%.
panels.code:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)
Z = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
panels.diagram: Scree plot: four bars (50, 31, 13, 6) with a cumulative line (50, 81, 94, 100) and a dashed 95% target line.

panels.heading: PCA Pitfalls
panels.body:
Not standardized: the largest-unit feature hijacks PC1.
Linear only: misses curved structure.
Components mix all features: hard to explain.
High variance is not always useful signal.
panels.diagram: Before/after: PC1 arrow pointing along a 'grams' axis when unscaled vs a balanced direction after scaling; orange warning icons.

panels.heading: t-SNE & UMAP for Pictures
panels.body:
t-SNE = t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding.
UMAP = uniform manifold approximation and projection.
Nonlinear: keep local neighbors together in 2D.
UMAP is faster and keeps more global layout. Use both for looking, not as model inputs.
panels.diagram: High-dimensional blob of colored points (MNIST-style digits) on the left; arrow to a 2D map with tight colored islands on the right.

panels.heading: Misreading the Map
panels.body:
Cluster sizes mean little: density gets equalized.
Gaps between clusters are not true distances.
Perplexity or n_neighbors reshape the picture: try several.
Random noise can form fake clusters.
panels.diagram: Same data rendered three ways (perplexity 5, 30, 100) giving visibly different layouts, stamped 'same data!'.

panels.heading: Selection vs Extraction
panels.body:
Selection: keep a subset of original columns (filters, L1, tree importance). Interpretable.
Extraction: build new features from all columns (PCA, autoencoders). Compact but abstract.
Need explanations? Select. Need compression? Extract.
panels.diagram: Left: table with some columns crossed out (selection). Right: all columns flowing into a funnel producing two new columns PC1, PC2 (extraction).

pages.footer: Use PCA to compress, t-SNE or UMAP to look, and never measure distances on a t-SNE plot.
pages.summary: Explains why high-dimensional data is hard (curse of dimensionality), how PCA finds directions of maximum variance with a worked explained-variance example, how t-SNE and UMAP make 2D pictures and how they are misread, and the difference between feature selection and feature extraction.

pages.title: BIAS, VARIANCE & REGULARIZATION
pages.subtitle: Find the sweet spot between too simple and too wiggly
pages.learner: Why does my test score drop?

panels.heading: Underfit vs Overfit
panels.body:
Underfit: high train error, high test error. Too simple.
Overfit: low train error, much higher test error. Memorized noise.
Good fit: both low and close together.
panels.diagram: Three plots of the same noisy points: a straight line (UNDERFIT), a smooth curve (GOOD), a wild degree-15 polynomial through every point (OVERFIT).

panels.heading: The Bias-Variance Trade-off
panels.body:
Expected error = bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise.
Bias: error from wrong assumptions.
Variance: sensitivity to which training sample you got.
More complexity: bias down, variance up -> U-shaped test error.
panels.diagram: Dartboard 2x2 (low/high bias x low/high variance) beside a plot of error vs model complexity: falling bias^2 curve, rising variance curve, U-shaped total with the sweet spot marked.

panels.heading: Learning Curves
panels.body:
Plot train and validation error vs training set size.
Both high and close: high bias -> add features or capacity.
Large gap that shrinks with data: high variance -> more data or regularize.
panels.diagram: Two learning-curve plots: HIGH BIAS (train and validation curves converge at a high error) and HIGH VARIANCE (big gap narrowing slowly as data grows).

panels.heading: L1 vs L2 vs Elastic Net
panels.body:
Add a penalty to the loss:
L2 (ridge): + lambda * sum(w^2). Shrinks all weights smoothly.
L1 (lasso): + lambda * sum(|w|). Drives many weights to exactly 0.
Elastic net: mixes both; good with correlated features.
panels.diagram: Classic 2D picture: elliptical loss contours meeting a diamond (L1, touching at a corner on an axis -> w2 = 0) and a circle (L2, touching off-axis).

panels.heading: Worked Example: 50 Features
panels.body:
100 rows, 50 features, only 5 matter.
Plain least squares: 50 noisy weights, overfits.
Ridge: 50 small nonzero weights.
Lasso: most weights exactly 0; the useful few survive.
panels.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet
Ridge(alpha=1.0); Lasso(alpha=0.1)
ElasticNet(alpha=0.1, l1_ratio=0.5)
panels.diagram: Three bar charts of 50 coefficients: OLS = tall random bars; ridge = all shrunk short; lasso = mostly flat zero with 5 lime bars standing.

panels.heading: Early Stopping
panels.body:
Track validation loss every epoch.
Stop after 'patience' epochs without improvement; restore the best weights.
Works like L2: weights cannot travel far from their start.
panels.diagram: Training loss falling steadily, validation loss U-shaped; a stop sign at the validation minimum labeled 'best checkpoint'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Tuning lambda on the test set: use validation or cross-validation.
Penalizing unscaled features: the penalty becomes unfair. Scale first.
sklearn alpha = penalty strength, but C in SVM and LogisticRegression is its inverse.
panels.diagram: Orange warning tags on a 'test set' lock, a lopsided scale, and a dial labeled 'C = 1 / lambda'.

panels.heading: Double Descent Note
panels.body:
Huge models can break the U: test error peaks where parameters ~ data points, then falls again as size grows.
The classic trade-off still guides most tabular models.
panels.diagram: Test error vs model size: classic U, a spike at the 'interpolation threshold', then a second descent to the right.

pages.footer: Diagnose first: high bias needs more capacity, high variance needs more data or regularization.
pages.summary: Explains underfitting vs overfitting, the bias-variance decomposition, how to read learning curves, L1 (lasso), L2 (ridge) and elastic net penalties with a worked example, early stopping, tuning pitfalls, and the double descent phenomenon in very large models.

pages.title: FEATURE ENGINEERING CHEAT SHEET
pages.subtitle: Better inputs beat fancier models
pages.learner: Why did my 99% model fail live?

panels.heading: Scaling & Standardization
panels.body:
Standardize: z = (x - mean) / std -> mean 0, std 1.
Min-max: (x - min) / (max - min) -> range 0 to 1.
Needed for k-NN, SVM, PCA, regularized and neural models. Trees don't care.
Outliers? Robust scaling or a log transform.
panels.diagram: Three histograms of the same feature: raw (0-200,000), standardized (centered at 0), min-max (squeezed into 0-1).

panels.heading: Encoding Categoricals
panels.body:
One-hot: red, green, blue -> red = [1, 0, 0]. Safe; explodes with many categories.
Ordinal: S < M < L -> 0, 1, 2. Only for ordered values.
Target encoding: replace each category with its mean target. Powerful, but risky.
panels.diagram: A 'color' column turning into three 0/1 columns; a 'size' column turning into 0/1/2; a 'city' column turning into decimal churn rates.

panels.heading: Target Encoding Risks
panels.body:
Computed on all rows, it leaks each row's own label.
A city with 1 customer who churned -> encoding 1.0 = the answer.
Fix: out-of-fold encoding plus smoothing toward the global mean.
panels.diagram: Table row 'city = Smalltown, n = 1, churned = 1 -> encoding 1.0' with an orange leak drip flowing from label to feature; fixed version shows a shrunk value near the global mean.

panels.heading: Missing Values
panels.body:
Ask why it's missing: missingness can be signal.
Impute median (numbers), most frequent or a 'missing' category (categories).
Add an is_missing indicator column.
Fit imputers on training data only.
panels.diagram: A table with blank cells being filled in cyan, plus a new lime 0/1 'is_missing' column added on the right.

panels.heading: Data Leakage
panels.body:
Leakage: training uses information unavailable at prediction time.
Target leakage: using 'refund_issued' to predict churn.
Contamination: scaling or imputing on all data before splitting.
Red flag: scores that look too good.
panels.diagram: Timeline with 'prediction moment' marker; a feature box sitting after the marker with an orange arrow sneaking back into the model.

panels.heading: Pipeline: Leak-Proof by Design
panels.body:
Every fit runs inside each CV fold, automatically.
The same steps run at prediction time.
panels.code:
num = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), StandardScaler())
pre = make_column_transformer((num, num_cols), (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols))
model = make_pipeline(pre, LogisticRegression())
cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)
panels.diagram: Flow diagram: raw columns -> numeric branch (impute, scale) and categorical branch (one-hot) -> merge -> model, all inside a box labeled 'refit per fold'.

panels.heading: Feature Selection
panels.body:
Filter: drop constant columns; rank by mutual information.
Wrapper: RFE (recursive feature elimination) with a model.
Embedded: L1 weights or tree importance.
Select inside the CV loop, or the scores lie.
panels.diagram: Funnel with three labeled layers (filter, wrapper, embedded) narrowing 100 columns to 12.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
One-hot on IDs: thousands of useless columns.
Unseen category at serving time -> crash: handle_unknown='ignore'.
Training-serving skew: compute features identically in both.
panels.diagram: Orange warning icons over an exploding column count, a crashing server, and two mismatched feature recipes labeled 'train' and 'serve'.

pages.footer: Fit every transform on training data only, and wrap it in a Pipeline so you can't forget.
pages.summary: Practical feature engineering: scaling and standardization, encoding categorical variables (one-hot, ordinal, target encoding and its leakage risk), handling missing values, spotting data leakage, building a leak-proof scikit-learn Pipeline, and selecting features without fooling yourself.
